excerpt_original: For the 10th edition of the Besançon Photography Festival, Mélanie Wenger is showing “Sugar Moon,” four years spent in Texas with Erik Grimland, a professional hunter and taxidermist, and his family. A deep dive into rural, pro-Trump America that neither pleads nor condemns.…

blocks.text: Hunting zebra in Texas? At first, the idea struck her as absurd. Mélanie Wenger, a graduate in literature and journalism, founding member of Inland and winner of the 2017 HSBC Prize for Photography, had by then spent years working on wildlife trafficking in Africa. In Zimbabwe, she followed an American elephant hunter who told her about Texas ranches where people shoot animals brought in from every continent. She looked into it, wrote to many landowners, combed through hunting forums. Only one replied: Erik Grimland. They agreed to meet at the international hunting convention in Dallas on January 3, 2018. “With no promises, I bought a one-way plane ticket to go and meet him,” she recalled.

The next day, Erik invited her to spend a few days at the Rockin G Ranch. She stayed a long time, came back, took few pictures. She had to wait, to “get past the American-style show.” A former police officer in Amarillo, one of the most violent cities in the country, and the son of an oil magnate, Erik knew people hated him for what he did. He said so over and over, almost as a routine, and didn’t care. The timing mattered. A few months earlier, Donald Trump had entered the White House, triggering, according to the photographer, “a kind of disinhibition of extreme ideologies, particularly around gun ownership and hunting.”

blocks.alt: A man carrying a mounted zebra trophy out of a trailer in front of a Texas house under a stormy sky
blocks.caption: Suburban Zebra © Mélanie Wenger / Inland

blocks.text: Their pact came down to three words: “Agree to disagree.” “We agreed on only one thing: the fact that we didn’t agree,” Mélanie Wenger summed up. Her frankness kept some ranches closed to her, an opaque world that does not open its doors to the press, but it also protected her. “My position was a kind of totem,” she said. “In a world where reality and truth are disappearing, holding on to the basics, to the foundations of journalistic ethics, became reassuring.” Being French helped (France was far away, and therefore less dangerous). “They probably saw my position as that charming but outdated thing from the Old Continent.” She still had to win over the clients and the transporters, one by one. Over time, she ended up “becoming part of the furniture.” The real test, though, took place elsewhere: handling a buffalo charge, getting very close to a frightened fawn, while Erik watched. “As if the animals could sense human nature, and it was they, in the end, who judged me worthy of trust.”

At the Rockin G Ranch, hunting was only a symptom. The real subject was a family. “In Erik, I found a captivating character, of course, but in his children, I found the face of a possible future America,” said the photographer, who also spoke of “an ideology built on nothing.” Sydney, a teenager and then a young adult, had her father’s temperament and an infinite love of horses. Which did not stop her from hanging a zebra trophy above her bed (“Sydney’s trophy”). She is now finishing her veterinary studies. Her brother, for his part, received a shotgun for Christmas the year Mélanie Wenger arrived. Tenderness and firepower, love and possession: it was this confusion that “bothered” her, and that she considers “far more universal than Texan.” If Erik allowed her to examine alpha-male culture, Sydney opened another question, that of women’s place in a deeply patriarchal world. “Through them, it is also tomorrow’s America that is at stake,” she said.

blocks.alt: A young woman holding a rifle on her bed next to a mounted zebra trophy
blocks.caption: Sydney’s Trophy © Mélanie Wenger / Inland

blocks.text: The images look composed, almost staged. They are not. “None of my images are staged. They are the result of several years of immersion, of discreet work,” Mélanie Wenger explained. No flash, no reflector, no work on the light, “no fashion language.” Always one step back. Beauty? Secondary. “It’s rather the surrealism, the never-seen (or barely seen) in ‘Sugar Moon’ that creates a reaction,” she said. Dystopian rather than aesthetic, her photographs do not make hunting seductive, “quite the opposite.” To each their own, she conceded, but for her, art must “create a visual and emotional shock that pushes people toward personal reflection.”

Pro-Trump America quickly emerged as the real phenomenon to tell. Erik launched into long monologues against climate change, wind turbines and migration, could fly into a black rage about the state of his country, never set foot in New York, let alone California. “Above all, he had grown up in a bubble, the Texas bubble,” said Mélanie Wenger, that of a rural America, not necessarily wealthy, from the Bible Belt, “that felt forgotten” and did not recognize itself in any political discourse. Her method is well established: a figure on the margins, the small story to tell the big one.

blocks.alt: A man in a cowboy hat feeding two giraffes in the morning mist on a Texas ranch
blocks.caption: Texan Giraffes © Mélanie Wenger / Inland

blocks.text: Produced by National Geographic and Le Figaro Magazine , and exhibited at Visa pour l’Image in 2021, the series has divided audiences. In France, it sparked debate, emotion, a form of understanding. But during one exhibition, partners pulled out and school visits were canceled. In the United States, the version broadcast by National Geographic was “heavily modified and sanitized,” turned into a more consensual exploration of the exotic animal industry. Over there, people rarely talk about what makes them angry. “Tick the boxes, A or B, good or bad, there’s no room for gray,” she said. Gray, precisely, is her material.

blocks.alt: A dead scimitar oryx lying in tall grass under a rainbow
blocks.caption: Oryx Down © Mélanie Wenger / Inland

blocks.text: Then there is the money. Mélanie Wenger does not claim to settle the matter; she lays out the contradiction: today, it is an animal’s value that guarantees its protection. Conservation, she pointed out, is largely funded by hunting, especially in Africa, where safari companies pay for anti-poaching efforts. In Texas, species that are extinct in their natural habitat survive, bred in semi-captivity, without biological monitoring or any guarantee of a return to the wild. But they exist. “It’s an obsessive quest for truth,” she said. “My job is to create this confrontation and leave viewers face to face with their own questions.”

“Sugar Moon” by Mélanie Wenger is on view at the Besançon Photography Festival from October 3 to November 20, 2026. Masterclass “Showing Your Documentary Work” : November 21–22 and December 12–13, 2026
